candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: perform medication reconciliation, identify adverse effects/interactions/duplication, monitor medication response, and provide safe medication teaching across transitions of care.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — older-adult polypharmacy and comprehensive medication review
candidate.educational_objective: Perform comprehensive medication review in older adults with polypharmacy by reconciling all prescription, OTC and supplement products and assessing ongoing need, interactions, adverse effects, duplication and medication-management burden.

options.A: Review the complete regimen—including prescriptions from all clinicians, OTC products, vitamins and supplements—for adverse effects, interactions, duplication, ongoing need, and medication-management problems.
options.B: Review only medications prescribed by the admitting clinician because drugs from other prescribers are outside the current medication review.
options.C: Stop the oldest medications first because duration of therapy is the primary criterion for deprescribing in polypharmacy.
options.D: Assume the regimen is safe when every drug was prescribed by a licensed clinician, even when several prescribers are involved.

candidate.rationale: The National Institute on Aging notes that older adults often take many medicines, which increases the risk of side effects, drug interactions, duplicate ingredients, and medication-management difficulties. NIA advises patients and clinicians to maintain and review a complete list that includes prescriptions from all prescribers, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, dietary supplements, and herbal remedies, and to ask whether every medicine is still needed. Therefore A is correct. B creates an incomplete reconciliation, C uses medication age rather than clinical indication/risk as the deprescribing criterion, and D incorrectly assumes multiple valid prescriptions cannot interact or duplicate therapy.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Older-adult polypharmacy requires comprehensive review of all prescription and nonprescription products for interactions, side effects, duplication, ongoing necessity and management problems rather than assuming safety because each medication was individually prescribed.
candidate.source_document_title: Taking Medicines Safely as You Age
candidate.source_locator: Medication safety sections: tell providers about all medicines including those prescribed by other doctors, OTC drugs, vitamins, supplements and herbal remedies; mixing products can cause serious problems. Keeping track: maintain a complete list. Do I need to take so many medications?: polypharmacy is a concern in older adults and taking many medications increases side-effect and unintended-problem risk; discuss whether any can safely be reduced/stopped.
candidate.source_version_date: Current NIA medication-safety guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidate.stem: An older adult takes twelve medications prescribed by several clinicians. Which concern should the nurse prioritize during medication review?
